scheme.mark_scheme:
- Matches can be correctly quoted and cited text / the bibliography / common phrases and terms (1)
- the teacher must check which parts match and whether they are acknowledged (1)
scheme.model_answer: Some of the matching text may be quotations with references, the reference list or common technical phrases, so the teacher must check each highlighted part to see whether it is acknowledged.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Compares the structure / logic of the programs, not just the text (1)
- so similarity is detected even when variable names / comments / spacing are changed; shows matching sections (1)
scheme.model_answer: It compares the structure of the code rather than the exact text, so it reports the programs as similar even though the variable names were changed, and highlights the matching sections.

prefill: The exact words of the author in quotation marks
The author's idea rewritten in your own words, about the same length

Any three (1 each): copyright is automatic when the work is created; author has economic and moral rights; permission / licence needed to copy, publish, adapt; quotation allowed with author and source; protection lasts life + 70 years; ideas / facts not protected; software protected — no copying without licence; licence conditions must be followed
scheme.model_answer: 1 Copyright applies automatically when a work is created. 2 Copying or publishing a work needs the owner's permission. 3 A quotation must name the author and the source.

questions.title: Registration
questions.text: A student's essay is only protected by copyright if it is registered with the state.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.

questions.title: Author's rights
questions.text: Explain the difference between an author's **economic** rights and **moral** rights.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Economic rights: to earn money from the work — sell, license, copy, distribute (1)
- Moral rights: to be named as the author and to protect the work from distortion / changes (1)
scheme.model_answer: Economic rights let the author earn money by selling or licensing copies; moral rights let the author be named as the creator and object to the work being changed or distorted.

questions.title: Checking a group project
questions.text:
Before submitting their research report, a group runs it through an anti-plagiarism checker. The report shows 42% similarity: most matches come from Wikipedia and from another school's report published online.

Discuss what the group should do before submitting, and how they should use sources correctly.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks:
- Look at each highlighted match / identify copied passages (1)
- Rewrite copied text in their own words (paraphrase) or put exact words in quotation marks (1)
- Cite every source in the text and in a reference list / bibliography (1)
- Do not use the other school's report without acknowledgement — it is someone else's work / copyright (1)
- Re-check the report after changes; exclude quotes / bibliography from the score (1)
[Max 4]
scheme.model_answer: The group should read every highlighted passage. Where they copied text, they should either rewrite it fully in their own words or put the exact words in quotation marks, and cite Wikipedia and the other school's report in the text and in the reference list. They must not present the other school's work as their own. Then they should run the check again.

summary: What plagiarism is and its forms, how anti-plagiarism resources check documents and how to read a similarity report, the limits of these tools, how to avoid plagiarism with quotation and citation, and the main rules of copyright protection.

blocks.content: **Presenting another person's work, words, ideas, images or code as your own**, without clearly **acknowledging the source**. It is a form of academic dishonesty and can also break **copyright** law.

blocks.title: Forms of plagiarism
rows: **Direct (copy-paste)**
Text is copied word for word without quotation marks or a reference
**Mosaic / patchwriting**
Phrases from several sources are mixed together with a few words changed
**Paraphrasing without citation**
Someone else's idea is rewritten in new words, but the source is not given
**Translation plagiarism**
A text in another language is translated and presented as original
**Self-plagiarism**
Re-using your own earlier work (e.g. a previous project) without permission or acknowledgement
**Code plagiarism**
Copying program code from a classmate or the Internet and changing variable names
**Ghost-writing / AI text**
Submitting work written by another person or by an AI tool as your own, when this is not allowed
**Incorrect citation**
Giving a wrong or incomplete source, so the reader cannot find the original

items.title: Why plagiarism is a problem
items.content:
- It is **dishonest** — the work does not show the student's own knowledge.
- It is **unfair** to the original author and to other students.
- The student **does not learn** the skills the task was designed to develop.
- Consequences: **zero marks**, disqualification from an exam or competition, loss of reputation, expulsion; in professional life — legal action for copyright infringement.

items.title: Why people plagiarise
items.content:
- Lack of time / poor planning.
- Not knowing how to **cite** or **paraphrase** correctly.
- Thinking that information on the Internet is free to use.
- Pressure to get high marks.

blocks.content: A program or online service that **compares a document with a very large database of texts** — web pages, books, journals and previously submitted student work — and produces a **similarity report** showing which parts match other sources.

blocks.title: How a document is checked
items: The user (or teacher) **uploads** the document (DOCX, PDF, TXT) or pastes the text.
The system breaks the text into **fragments** (sequences of words, "shingles") and creates **digital fingerprints** of them.
The fingerprints are **compared** with its databases: the Internet, academic publications, its archive of submitted papers.
**Matching fragments are highlighted**, and each match is linked to its **source**.
A **similarity (originality) score** in % is calculated, and a **report** is produced.

blocks.title: Examples of anti-plagiarism resources
rows: **Turnitin**
Used by universities and schools worldwide; large archive of student papers; teachers see the report
**Antiplagiat** (antiplagiat.ru)
Widely used in Kazakhstan and Russia; checks Russian- and Kazakh-language texts
**Unicheck**, **Copyleaks**, **Plagscan**
Online checkers for schools and companies
**Grammarly Plagiarism Checker**, free online checkers
Quick checks against web pages (smaller databases)
**MOSS**, **JPlag**
Detect similar **program code**, even when variable names are changed
**Google search**
Searching an exact phrase in quotation marks shows whether it exists online

blocks.title: Reading a similarity report
blocks.content:
| Source | Match |
|---|---|
| 1. en.wikipedia.org — "Database normalization" | 12 % |
| 2. Student paper, NIS Almaty, 2025 | 9 % |
| 3. textbook "Computer Science 11", p. 87 | 4 % |
| **Total similarity** | **25 %** |

The highlighted text shows **which sentences** match. The teacher then checks whether each match is **properly quoted and cited** (acceptable) or **copied without acknowledgement** (plagiarism).

items.title: Interpreting the score correctly
items.content:
- A similarity score is **not** a plagiarism score — it only shows **matching text**.
- Correctly **quoted and referenced** passages, the **bibliography**, common phrases and technical terms also produce matches.
- Most checkers let the user **exclude quotes and the reference list** from the score.
- A **high score with no citations** needs investigation; even a **low score** can hide paraphrased plagiarism.

items.title: Limitations of anti-plagiarism software
items.content:
- Cannot detect copying from **sources not in its database** (printed books, private documents).
- Can be fooled by heavy **paraphrasing**, synonym-replacing tools or translation.
- Does not check **images, diagrams** or ideas well.
- **False positives** — common phrases, names, standard definitions.
- Uploaded work may be **stored** by the service — privacy and copyright of the student's own work.
- A human must always **interpret** the report.

blocks.title: Checking your own work before submitting
items: Use the school's checker (or a free one) on the **final draft**.
If it is a quotation — add **quotation marks** and a **reference**.
If it is your paraphrase of a source — make sure the source is **cited**; rewrite more in your own words if it is too close.
Check that the **reference list** contains every source.

blocks.title: Quoting, paraphrasing and summarising
rows: **Quotation**
The **exact words**, in **quotation marks**
**Yes** — with the page if possible
**Paraphrase**
The idea rewritten **completely in your own words and structure**
**Yes**
**Summary**
The **main points** of a longer text, much shorter, in your own words
**Yes**
Common knowledge
Facts widely known (e.g. "Astana is the capital of Kazakhstan")
No

blocks.title: Citing a source (Harvard / APA style)
blocks.content:
In the text: *Normalisation reduces data redundancy (Connolly and Begg, 2015).*

In the reference list: *Connolly, T. and Begg, C. (2015) Database Systems. 6th edn. Harlow: Pearson.*

A web page: *Microsoft (2026) "Create a table of contents". Available at: support.microsoft.com (Accessed: 10 October 2026).*

Keep a list of every source **while you research** (author, title, date, URL), write notes **in your own words**, and use the word processor's **References** tools (citations, bibliography, footnotes).

The **exclusive legal right of the author** (or owner) of an original work — text, software, music, images, films, websites — to **copy, distribute, adapt, publish and perform** it, and to allow or forbid others to do so.

blocks.title: The main rules of copyright protection
rows: **Copyright is automatic**
A work is protected **from the moment it is created** — no registration is needed; the © sign is optional but useful
**The author owns the rights**
**Economic rights** (to earn money from copies, licences) and **moral rights** (to be named as the author, to protect the work from distortion)
**Protection lasts for a limited time**
In Kazakhstan and many countries: the author's **life + 70 years**; afterwards the work enters the **public domain**
**Permission is needed**
To copy, publish, translate, adapt or sell a work you need the **owner's permission** or a **licence**
**Ideas and facts are not protected**
Copyright protects the **expression** (the text, code, image), not the idea itself
**Limited free use is allowed**
**Quotation** for study, criticism, news or teaching is allowed **with the author's name and source** and only to a justified extent
**Software is protected like a literary work**
Copying, distributing or installing software without a **licence** is illegal
**Licences set the conditions**
E.g. **Creative Commons** (BY — credit the author, NC — non-commercial, ND — no changes, SA — share alike); open-source licences (GPL, MIT)
**Breaking copyright has consequences**
Removal of content, fines, compensation to the owner, criminal liability for serious cases

blocks.title: The law in Kazakhstan
blocks.content: Copyright is protected by the **Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan "On Copyright and Related Rights"** and the **Civil Code**. Computer programs and databases are protected works.

blocks.title: Using other people's work in a school project
rows: Quote two sentences from a book
They are in **quotation marks** with a **reference**
Use a photo from a website
It has a **Creative Commons** or free licence (follow its conditions) or you have **permission**
Use a song in a video
It is **royalty-free / licensed**, or you have permission
Use code from an online tutorial
Its licence allows it, and you **credit** the author in comments
Use a classmate's work
**Never** as your own work

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe how anti-plagiarism software checks a document. [3]**
The text is **compared with a large database** of web pages, publications and submitted work (1); **matching fragments are highlighted** with links to their sources (1); a **similarity percentage / report** is produced (1).

**Q: Explain why a similarity score of 25% does not always mean that the student has plagiarised. [2]**
Matches may be **correctly quoted and cited** passages, the **reference list** or common phrases (1); the teacher must look at **which parts** match and whether they are acknowledged (1).

**Q: Name two copyright protection rules. [2]**
Copyright arises **automatically** when the work is created (1); a work may be **copied or published only with the owner's permission / licence**; quotations must name the **author and source**; protection lasts for the author's life + 70 years (1).

- Saying that changing a few words makes copied text your own — it is still plagiarism without a citation.
- Treating the similarity % as proof of plagiarism.
- Thinking that copyright must be **registered** — it is automatic.
- Thinking that everything on the Internet is in the **public domain**.
